title: UK Universities Withdraw Offers to Indian and Other Students as Visa Refusals Rise
excerpt: With sponsor licences now at risk above a 5% visa refusal rate, universities are revoking offers pre-emptively — withdrawn applications from Indian students rose to 5.2% in the first half of 2026.
body:
• UK universities are withdrawing admission offers from applicants in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nigeria to protect their student-sponsor licences.
  • Since June 1, universities must keep visa refusal rates below 5% — down from 10% — enrol at least 95% of sponsored students and maintain an 85% course-completion rate.
  • Withdrawn study-visa applications from Indian students rose from 1.2% to 5.2% in a year; Pakistan hit 40.9%, Bangladesh 23.5% and Nigeria 22.7%.
  • If you hold a UK offer, confirm your CAS status directly with the university now — a withdrawn offer cancels the linked visa application.

Offers pulled before visas are even decided

British universities are withdrawing admission offers from international students — including Indians — because rising visa refusal rates now threaten the licences that allow them to recruit overseas at all. A Financial Times analysis of Home Office data found that 10.5 percent of UK study-visa applications were withdrawn in the first half of 2026, up from 2.3 percent in the same period of 2025 and just 0.4 percent in 2023.

The distinction matters: a withdrawal is not a refusal. An application is withdrawn when it is discontinued before a decision — and universities themselves say the surge largely reflects institutions revoking offers and sponsorship pre-emptively, before the Home Office can refuse a visa and damage their compliance record.

The 5 percent line universities cannot cross

Under the tightened Basic Compliance Assessment in force since June 1, a university whose sponsored students exceed a 5 percent visa refusal rate — halved from the previous 10 percent — risks losing its sponsor licence. Schools must also enrol at least 95 percent of the students they sponsor and keep course completion at 85 percent or above. Enroly data cited in sector reporting suggests refusal rates at nearly half of universities already exceed the new threshold.

The universities of Sunderland, Chester, Wolverhampton, East London, Coventry and Hertfordshire, along with Oxford Brookes and Glasgow Caledonian, are among those that have tightened recruitment. Around 15 universities are believed to have suspended recruitment from Pakistan entirely this year, and Oxford Brookes has paused some sponsorship from Bangladesh and Pakistan while adding compliance checks for applicants from Nigeria and India.

"Our visa system must not be used as a backdoor to asylum and illegal working."

— Mike Tapp, UK Migration and Citizenship Minister

What Indian applicants should do

India's withdrawal rate, at 5.2 percent, is far below Pakistan's 40.9 percent, and there is no blanket ban on Indian students. But the direction is clear: offers are now conditional on a university's risk appetite, not just a student's merit. Applicants for the January and September intakes should confirm with the university's international office that their Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS) is active, keep financial documentation ready to the standard described in the official UK student visa guidance, and ask directly whether their course or nationality faces additional screening. Families weighing the UK against Canada, Australia or the US should factor in this new friction: a strong file matters more than ever, and applying to more than one university is now risk management, not extravagance.

Why the government is tightening

Ministers say the rules target abuse of the student route by people who enter on study visas and then claim asylum or work illegally. Universities, for their part, warn the policy threatens their finances — international fees make up roughly 23 percent of sector income — and that blunt nationality-based screening punishes genuine students for the actions of a minority. The Home Office publishes its sponsor guidance for institutions at gov.uk, and further compliance changes are expected as the refusal data for the second half of 2026 comes in.
